MEET FRIDGEMATE

Small changes.
Smarter habits.

FridgeMate is a student project exploring how a mobile interface could make a smart refrigerator easier to manage. It brings useful information into one clear place — from food inventory to temperature and energy insights.

The current version is a demonstration concept. The interface uses sample data and does not connect to a physical refrigerator.

A Fridge That Works for You

An organized refrigerator makes it easier to find ingredients, plan meals and see what needs using. You do not need expensive organizers to make a difference.

Create easy-to-understand zones

Group similar products together, while following food-safety guidance for safe shelf placement and separation of raw and ready-to-eat foods.

Keep the important things visible

Place ingredients you plan to use soon where you will notice them. Clear containers and simple labels can help, but an uncluttered shelf is often enough.

Label leftovers

Write down what is inside a container and when it was prepared. This makes it easier to plan your next meal and follow safe storage recommendations.

Reset your fridge before shopping

Take a few minutes to check your shelves, wipe spills and note what is running low. You can then build a shopping list based on what is actually missing.

Make your system easy to maintain

The best organization system is the one you will use consistently. FridgeMate explores a digital overview that could complement a simple physical layout.

A little structure can turn your refrigerator from a mystery into a useful part of your daily routine.

Small Habits for a More Efficient Kitchen

A more efficient kitchen often begins with ordinary habits. A few simple checks can make appliances easier to maintain and their energy use easier to understand.

Be mindful of the refrigerator door

Know what you need before opening the door and avoid leaving it open unnecessarily. Follow your appliance manufacturer’s instructions for temperature settings.

Keep appliances in good condition

Clean surfaces, inspect refrigerator door seals and follow maintenance and ventilation recommendations from the manufacturer.

Understand patterns over time

A single energy reading may not tell you much. Trends over several days or weeks can be more informative, especially when compared under similar conditions.

Bring information together

FridgeMate explores an energy dashboard that presents consumption trends alongside other refrigerator information. In the current student prototype, these values are illustrative rather than live measurements.

Smart living is about using information well. Small habits and clear feedback can support better decisions over time.

Plan Meals Around What You Already Have

Meal planning can be flexible rather than strict. Start with the ingredients already in your kitchen and build a few practical meals around them.

Step 1: Take inventory

Check your fridge, freezer and pantry before choosing recipes. Make a short note of ingredients that need using soon.

Step 2: Choose flexible meal ideas

A soup, pasta dish, rice bowl or salad can often accommodate different vegetables and proteins. Flexible meals are easier to adapt when plans change.

Step 3: Make a focused shopping list

After deciding on a few meals, list only what you still need. This can help avoid buying another item that is already waiting at home.

Step 4: Prepare only what is helpful

Washing suitable produce, portioning ingredients or preparing a few components can save time. Store prepared food safely and follow recommended storage periods.

Step 5: Leave room for real life

You do not have to plan every meal. Keep a few flexible options and adjust the week when needed. FridgeMate explores how an inventory and shopping list could work together.

A good meal plan should make your week easier, not more complicated.

5 Simple Ways to Keep Your Food Fresh for Longer

A little attention to storage and planning can help your groceries stay useful for longer. Here are five approachable habits to bring into your kitchen.

1. Start with the right storage

Different ingredients need different conditions. Keep perishable foods refrigerated according to their labels and local food-safety guidance. Store dry goods in suitable cupboards and keep containers closed when appropriate.

2. Give your fridge a simple layout

Put frequently used ingredients in easy-to-reach places and keep foods you want to use soon clearly visible. A consistent layout helps you find things quickly and notice what is missing.

3. Check dates, but understand the labels

Look at use-by and best-before dates when planning meals. A use-by date is about safety; a best-before date generally relates to quality. Always follow relevant food-safety instructions.

4. Plan around what you already own

Before going shopping, take a quick look through the fridge. Try building one or two meals around ingredients you already have. This helps reduce duplicate purchases and forgotten food.

5. Make a short weekly check a habit

A five-minute fridge review can help you plan the week, wipe up spills and update your shopping list. FridgeMate explores how a digital food inventory and reminders could support this routine.

Keeping food fresh does not require a perfect system. Small, repeatable steps are often the easiest place to begin.

Less Food Waste Starts with Knowing What You Have

Reducing food waste begins with awareness. When you know what is in your kitchen, you can make more thoughtful choices about what to buy and cook.

See what is already in your fridge

Food often gets overlooked because it is hidden behind other items. Try keeping a simple inventory or placing ingredients that need attention at the front.

Shop with a flexible plan

Think about a few meals you could make during the week, then write down only the ingredients you need. Leave some flexibility for changes in your schedule.

Give leftovers a second purpose

Leftover vegetables can become soup or a stir-fry, while cooked grains may work in a bowl or salad. Store leftovers safely and use them within recommended timeframes.

Use reminders as helpful prompts

A reminder about an upcoming date can encourage you to plan ahead. FridgeMate is designed around the idea of making those prompts easy to find in one place.

Progress matters more than perfection. One better shopping list or one well-used leftover meal is a useful start.

What Makes a Kitchen Feel Truly Smart?

A smart kitchen is not simply a room filled with connected devices. It is a space where technology helps people make everyday decisions with less effort.

Useful information, not more complexity

A helpful app should show the essentials clearly. You should not have to navigate through several menus just to check a basic status or find an ingredient.

One place for everyday tasks

Food inventory, temperature monitoring and energy information are easier to understand when they share a consistent interface. This is one of the main design ideas behind FridgeMate.

Technology that supports routines

A shopping list is useful before a trip to the store. An expiration reminder matters when planning dinner. Good technology fits the moment when information is needed.

Our FridgeMate prototype

FridgeMate is a student project exploring a mobile interface for an existing smart refrigerator. The current app demonstrates its features with example data and is not yet connected to a real appliance.

The goal is simple: make technology feel less like another task and more like a practical everyday assistant.
